title: Supply Chain Security - The Ultimate Guide to Software Composition Analysis (SCA) Tools

chunks.text: So, what is software composition analysis or SCA? Well, in security, this is a tool that helps keep your supply chain safe. In this video, we're going to dive into exactly what it is. We're going to look at the different types of tooling that is available and where it fits into your development life cycle.

My name is McKenzie and you are watching Tool Time by Aikido Security. SCA or software composition analysis can go by a couple of names. Open source dependency scanning, dependency scanning, supply chain security scanning, all these different types of areas, but essentially they're all the

same thing. What an SCA tool does is it looks at your application and all of the dependencies, the open source dependencies that make your application tick and scans them for vulnerabilities. Now, you may or may not know this, but around about 70 to 90% of all of the code that makes your application run

comes from open-source dependencies. So, if you're watching this on YouTube, presumably around about 70 to 90% of what makes YouTube YouTube comes from open-source packages. Now, this is great for a number of reasons. It's great because we can move quickly. It's why we're able to keep pushing the

boundaries of what we can do in applications. We don't need to reinvent the wheel every time we do it. But it does come at a risk. And that is that that big chunk of our application that we don't control can also have security vulnerabilities. And because we don't control it, we have limited ability to

be able to resolve them. Now, at first, thinking about open source dependencies feels easy because there's a whole bunch of dependencies that you know about because you introduced them. But there's a challenge. Just like your application runs on open source software, so does open source software run on open source

software. So we end up with this Russian nesting doll situation. Well, we may introduce one packet, but that might introduce several other packages that live inside it, which may introduce other packages, so on and so forth. So if we think about it back to YouTube, if we wanted to create a video streaming

service, then we would probably take some open source packages to help us play videos on our website. But inside those, there may be packages that enable audio streaming and video streaming. And then inside those there may be a whole bunch of different packages that do various different jobs of that like data

streaming or dealing with loads. Now why this all matters is if one of these dependencies ends up having a vulnerability within it, it can have a flow on effect. I'll give you a concrete example. There's a package called log 4j. It's a logging application for Java. In 2021, it was discovered that there

was a critical remote code execution vulnerability inside log forj. Well, log forj is something that we would call a foundational project. What that means is it's pretty much in everything because it was in everything. Once this vulnerability became public, then nearly the entire internet was vulnerable to

remote code execution through this. Now, you may have the question of why is it the entire internet and not just Java applications? Well, that's because we layer things on top of each other. Even if we have an application in Python or JavaScript, it probably sits on foundations of cloud architecture, of

infrastructure that uses various different languages. So, the whole supply chain can be very complicated and very convoluted. To help us make sense of all of this, SCA tools will first identify all of the packages that we have in our application and then check to see if there's any known issues or

vulnerabilities within it. A good SEA tool will look at frontier dependencies, but also transitive dependencies as well. I'm going to take just a very quick side quest here because there's something else called an esbomb. Now, ESBOMs are very closely related to SEA, so I don't want to do an entire video

about it, but an ESBOM stands for software bill of materials. And essentially what this is is a document that you can share with people that looks at all of the open source packages inside your application and the versions that they have. This is important because sometimes for compliance, you

need to provide this to certain parties when they're choosing to use your your your application. And I'm specifically looking at legislation that involves government contracts. So while we sometimes have different tools for sbombs, generally speaking, an SCA tool will come with a component that can

generate this software bill of material. All right, side quest done. Back to back to understanding SCA. Let's first start by exploring how we can see what dependencies we have in our application. Well, there's a couple of files. If you're dealing in JavaScript or Node, you're going to have a package.json

file. This is what we have our frontier dependencies, direct dependencies. And then we also have a package-lock.json file. And this will have kind of transitive dependencies in them. If you look at the difference, the package.json file may only be kind of several lines long. Whereas the package lock.json file

may be thousands of lines of long because it has thousands of packages. This is built automatically. We don't create these like with all the dependencies we have in them. Now depending on what language you use, these files will be different. In Python, it's requirements.ext. You also might have a pip lock file. we're

dealing in Ruby, you have a gems file and a gems lock file and there's various different types of files that we deal with. You can kind of dive into what it is that you're programming in and what files you have for you there. But essentially, this is can be the first way that we can have a look inside of

our applications. Now, to understand the security part, I'm sorry, we have to do another side quest. We're doing a side quest. It calls something called CVE Commer vulnerabilities and exposure. And what happens in security is when we discover that there is a vulnerability inside an open- source package or a

popular software version, we create a CVE number. So I talked about log forj already. This is the CVE number for log forj. And what this saying is in specific versions of log forj, we have this critical vulnerability. Now, what is useful about this is that we can check databases with all of these CVE

numbers in there and we can check does our project contain a dependency that matches this CVE number or match the the the version in the CVE number. So, there's a couple of big databases. There's the NVD, the National Vulnerability Database. There's the MIT CVE database and there's the GitHub

advisory database. And there's a few more as well. Does this application contain a vulnerable version? So, let's have a look at that. I want to start by using a great open-source SCA tool called Trivy. And what we're going to do is we have this dummy project here, and we're just going to run Trivy, run a

scan of Trivy. And Trivy is going to look at our our dependencies. It's going to look at the databases, and it's going to tell us if we have a match. And obviously, as you can see here, we have lots and lots of matches. Now, we can export this in a JSON file if we want. we can put it in some kind of viewer.

Maybe we can sort it between what are the most critical vulnerabilities and we can start going through it. So now that we have our results from Trivia, what do we actually do? How do we solve these? Well, solving them is also simple. At least so it seems on the surface. All we do is we upgrade from a vulnerable

version to a nonvulnerable version. Where this becomes not so simple is that when upgrading breaks our application. Now, as you can see in this case, we have hundreds of these vulnerabilities. If we upgrade all of these, we're going to spend months quite literally trying to resolve all the issues that this

creates because it may break the functionality and it also could break the functionality of the dependencies that it relies on. So, there can be very very complicated to actually try and fix them. Now, that's not always true. Sometimes you can just upgrade and it works and it's perfect. In that case,

it's what we say that there's no breaking changes. In all other cases, we say that there's breaking changes, which means we can't easily upgrade them. So, what do we do in that situation? Well, we're going to come back to that side quest later, but for now, let's just talk about the results that we have.

Most of these are actually false positives. How on earth are these false positives? Well, it comes back to what we call reachability. The first example that I want to give you is what we call a dev dependency. And a dev dependency is basically a dependency that's not being used in the production of our

application, but usually being used in the build process and not in the runtime process. But that means there's nothing there for an attacker to exploit. The other reason why we get false positives are because the packages aren't what we call reachable. And usually this relates to how the package is introduced into

our application. So usually there's something called a package tree or a called tree. And what we can do is we can see that this dependency has introduced this dependency blah blah blah and we get all the way down to here throughout that tree. It may be that this ends dependency that is vulnerable

can be reached or it can't be but we can't figure that out without doing investigation. One particular way that this may be true is if the package that we're talking about has a vulnerability but it's a certain function. I I'll give you example in node projects. This is a very popular package called Y18N. Now,

this is just a barebones initialization library, but it has tens of millions of weekly downloads. This is a foundational project. It's probably in most node applications. Now, there's known vulnerabilities in this. One of the known vulnerabilities that we have here is a prototype pollution vulnerability

that scores 98 out of 100. This is about as critical as you can get. So, obviously, Logic would say that we don't want this in our project. However, maybe it's doing something really important. Maybe a whole bunch of other stuff depends on it, which in this case is true. Now, there's a certain function

that allows this prototype vulnerability to happen. That function is called set local. So, let's say the scenario that our application is using this and it's a transitive dependency. So, it's downstream. What we may discover is that at no point is the function set local used or called by any other dependencies or our

application. Now that means that what makes this vulnerable isn't true for our application. So we could ignore it. But again, how do we find this out? Well, we have to do a lot of deep diving into how our application works to find it. But let's bring up Aikido Security and have a look at some of this. So the the first

thing that I want to point to is that call tree. In my dashboard, I've narrowed down the results to just SCA. And so here we can see all the dependencies that we have. But at the top corner we have auto ignored. So you can see that here. And then we can click on the reason why this is ignored. And

we can see that there's various here. Dependency is not used in production. Affected function is not used. So like all there's all of these different various reasons of why we could ignore it. So this actually gets rid of around about 80% of all of the results that we have. Sometimes more, sometimes less.

None of this is magic. It's going to depend on your application, right? But if we click on some of this dependency not in use, what we can do is we can click on here it says reach re uh reachability analysis and we can actually see that call tree that I was talking about. Sometimes that call tree

is is small. This is the this is the package that we're that we introduced. These are the other packages that were introduced because of that. Sometimes it's ginormous like in this case you can see there's this massive call tree that we have. But the point is is that it's understanding how everything is used and

therefore is able to understand the process of how our application is using it. And this is why it's able to get rid of a lot of those alerts because it understands that this may be behind a dev tool that this isn't actually in production or that it can even understand if we click here the affected

function is not as use. I'll go to the example that I used before of Y18N. We can look at this. We can see yep the function that's vulnerable is set local. we're not using that. So, doesn't matter about the call tree that we're using. Uh we're not actually using that. And of course, it checks that in all of the uh

the packages that we have. The other area that's really important is that if we go back to uh our results, we can see here under the fix. Now, the fix is giving us say, hey, we need to upgrade to this latest version to fix this. Right? That's very cool. But we can see here this little

kind of caution symbol. What this says is this letting us know that there's a breaking change. That means that if we upgrade to the version that we need to to get rid of the vulnerability, it's going to break our application. Now, this is really important because we can actually see all of the all of the

packages that don't have that and then upgrade it. So, we can immediately get very quickly ahead and then we only need to focus on the few that actually have breaking changes. And the final thing that modern SCA tools will all typically have is something called autofix. And this is essentially creating the code

So autofix is kind of great and this is when you need the additional context of what's going to break uh and areas like that because now you can just automatically upgrade everything that's not going to break within a couple of clicks of the button and you can go on

title: HTTP Secure Headers for Web App Security | CORS, CSP, HSTS and more

chapters.label: Why Headers Matter for Web App Security
Wrap-up: Secure Your App by Default

chunks.text: Most developers lock down their back end but miss a simple trick on the front end. HTTP secure headers. For example, CSP helps stops things like cross-ite scripting. HSTS make sure your site always loads over HTTPS. And then there is course or COS, referral policy, permissions policy and more. Each

closing a different security loophole. These headers are built into the browser. You just have to use them right. In this video, you'll learn exactly what secure headers are, why they are critical, and how to quickly implement them, making your apps dramatically safer. Let's dive in.

Secure headers are tiny rule books your server sends to the browser, telling it how to treat your content securely. They don't touch your app logic, but they quietly enforce critical rules in the browser like only load scripts from trusted resources, always use HTTPS or don't leak sensitive referral data. And

just like that, you have shut down entire classes of attacks without changing a single line of JavaScript. Let's start with one of the most powerful content security policy or CSP. CSP is like a white list for your front end. It tells your browser only load scripts, styles, and assets from these

trusted places. For example, this says load everything from your own domain by default. Scripts can also come from your trusted CDN and block object tags entirely. No flash, no surprises. So without CSP, malicious scripts can run via XSS. Attackers can load code from any domain and plugins like Flash may

execute. With CSP, only trusted scripts are allowed. Browsers block unknown sources and risky elements are blocked. One pro tip, start with content security policy report only. It logs violations without blocking anything, so you can test it safely. Now, let's talk about HSTS. Some websites still load over plain HTTP

if the browser doesn't start with HTTPS. And that's a problem because in that initial moment, the connection is still unencrypted. That tiny window where the browser first reaches out over HTTP is all an attacker needs. On a public Wi-Fi network, someone could intercept the request, redirect you, or inject malicious

content before the site even switches to HTTPS. HSTS fixes this. Once the browser sees the HSTS header, it knows always use HTTPS for this domain. No exceptions. And here is what it looks like. This tells the browser, enforce HTTPS for one full year, include all subdomains. And preload this rule into browsers so even

firsttime visitors connect securely. It's a small header with a big impact, shutting down a common attack vector most people don't even realize exists. Next up is a small header that blocks a surprisingly sneaky attack, MIME sniffing. Let's say your server sends a file with a .txt extension, but inside

that file is actually some malicious JavaScript. Some older or lenient browsers might try to guess what kind of file it is and decide, hm, this looks like a script. Let me run it. That's called mimen sniffing and it can lead to unexpected script execution. even if the content type says otherwise. To prevent

this, we use Xc content type options no sniff. This tells the browser, trust what I said the file is. Don't try to guess. It's simple and it blocks a whole class of attacks where the browser gets a little too smart for its own good. Without this header, browser may sniff file types and misinterpret them or a

txt file with script content might get executed. So this header makes browsers strictly follow declared content type and malicious files are treated as plain text not scripts. Now when a user clicks a link from your site to another the browser sends a referral header. Basically saying hey this is where the

user came from. But here's the catch. That header might include full URLs including query parameters, tokens or even user ids. And that's risky. You might be leaking sensitive info to third party websites without even realizing it. To control this, we use referral policy strict origin when cross

origin. This means if the next page is on your own domain, send the full URL. If it's going to another domain, just send the origin, say bitemong.io, and nothing more. chunks.text: if you're building a product that requires logging in you probably have to deal with storing passwords but storing passwords opens you up to security risks like someone breaking into your database stealing all your passwords and dealing immense reputational damage to your product so how do you store passwords in a

secure fashion let's start from the worst way and steadily work our way up to something a little more secure i'm going to assume you have a little bit of software engineering knowledge let's go the ftr way to store your passwords is like normal data in a normal column perhaps with the rest of your user data

sometimes this is called storing passwords in plain text this is pretty bad because if a hacker gains access to your database they can steal all the passwords effortlessly security is all about multiple lines of defense and storing passwords in plain text is not a defense if your database is breached you're done

and database breaches happen quite often that's why this is f-tier but how can we do better if you watched my encryption video you might think that we should encrypt these passwords that's definitely an improvement because if they break into your database they get gibberish instead of useful information

however if they do get access to the key then they can decrypt all the passwords and you're unfortunately right back to ftr it's definitely nicer that the passwords aren't just sitting out there in the open but if a hacker has access to your database already it may not be much more

effort for them to steal the decryption key too from an adjacent server or config file also storing passwords in a way that makes it possible to retrieve the password increases the risk of an inside job where an employee with privileged access to the key decrypts people's passwords for

nefarious purposes the expert protection certainly helps but this is the tier how do we get to see the key insight is that we only need to know when the user types in the same password as when they signed up we don't actually need to know the password itself you might think the two are one of the same but they actually

aren't it's possible to take a password and generate a fingerprint from it which will let us know if we encounter the same password in the future but still be unable to recover the password directly from the fingerprint this is a technique known as hashing how do we use hashing when the user signs up we take the

password they provide generate a small fingerprint or hash and store it instead of the actual password in the future when the user tries to log in we take the password they typed in run the same hashing process and see if the output hashes compare if the hashes are the same it's overwhelmingly likely that they typed in

the correct password thanks to the power of hashing we're able to verify someone's password without storing the actual password hashing might sound a little magical at the moment how does hashing prevent someone from recovering their original password from the output hash and how does it prevent two strings from

hashing to the same thing and allowing someone to log in with the wrong password for the first one how to prevent someone from recovering the original password the process of hashing involves a lot of aggressive mixing of the data in the original input to produce the output it's like taking three paints of

different colors and mixing them together which probably results in some weird shade of brown with just the brown you'll probably be unable to guess the original three colors that made the brown in the same way you can't figure out the original password from the hash because the bits in the data have all been

thoroughly mixed and scrambled this property is known as being a one-way function like a one-way street once you hash you can't unhash for the second which is how hashing makes it hard for two strings to hash to the same value known as a hash collision the answer is similar to what i just said

the hash function mixes the data in such a way that even small tweaks in the input result in totally different hashes as a result for good hash functions there is no publicly known way to generate two strings whose hashes collide without just trying many many many strings no luck with these ten this property is

called collision resistance picking the right hash function is important we used to think that older hash functions that you may have heard about like md5 and sha-1 had collision resistance but cryptographic progress marches on and they've been proved insecure for example about a decade ago

researchers published a method for generating a collision two strings that have the same md5 hash that you can run in about a second on your laptop so we've moved on to stronger hash functions like sha2 which is the one i've been using in this video with our new hashing technique under our

belt let's hash all the passwords in our database instead of encrypting them to arrive at cd or password storage now we don't have a key that effortlessly unlocks the password table like before which is definitely an improvement however we need to talk about dictionary attacks as it turns out many people use

extremely weak passwords like password or one two three four five six if a hacker has access to your database they can just run your hash function on password or one two three four five six to get the hash and then find all the hashes that match in your database voila they've broken those people's passwords

this is called a dictionary attack because you could run through the dictionary hashing words as you go and seeing if any of them match the hash remember that it's not possible to directly turn a hash back into a password in general however because the hacker knows the hash came from a password

they can use their knowledge of human nature to narrow down the possible guesses which makes guessing feasible furthermore they can use lists of the most common passwords to pre-generate a huge database of hashes so all they need to do is to compare their huge database to your database to find matches

these databases are known as rainbow tables how can we defend against this let's go to b-tier for a technique that protects against rainbow tables but not against dictionary attacks it's a technique called salting when the user signs up rather than directly hashing each password we can first generate a short

random string called the salt then we prepend it to the string before running the hash we then store the salt next to the hashed password when the user logs in we can prepend the remembered salt to the password they entered and hash to see if it matches the stored password it's important to use the same salt at

login that was generated during signup which is why we want to store it in the database otherwise the user wouldn't be able to log in even with the right password because the hashes wouldn't match this makes rainbow tables useless because their databases only contain non-salted hashes for example these

users have the password qwerty but the table doesn't match anymore this has the added benefit of decorating users who have the same password previously if two users use the same password their hashes would be the same which is not ideal because you can see that they have the same password even if

you don't know what the password actually is now even though their passwords are the same their salts are different so the hashes are different but why is this still beat here remember the other issue we talked about which is dictionary attacks an attacker with a list of common passwords can still try all of them

against the hash using the salt they don't get the benefit of precomputation but they can still start from scratch furthermore specialized hardware like gpus have made it possible for people to compute billions of hashes per second which translates into billions of guests per second

how on earth do we stop this one let's see what a tier has to say an a tier is using a specialized password hashing function that is deliberately slow the previous hash functions we discussed are designed to be fast because they're used for other applications besides passwords password hashing functions like bcrypt

script and argon 2 come with salting for free and more importantly are designed to be really really really slow to consume lots of power and to take lots of memory it sounds weird but this is actually on purpose to defend against the overwhelming power of hardware the billions of hashes per second we saw

a moment ago can be slowed down to mere thousands per second if not even slower because you can actually choose the level of slowness you want this is known as the work factor with only thousands of guesses per second that's still enough to easily go through the most common passwords

but it's not enough to break tougher or more obscure passwords with the high enough work factor hackers might be able to break some of the passwords in your system but not all of them after all the goal of security is not to be immune to attacks which is impossible but to hinder attackers enough that they

turn their attention to other places as a concrete example let's look at bcrypt the output of b crypt looks like this it has a prefix that identifies the output as a decrypted thing a work factor a 22 character salt and a 31 character hash the most interesting thing about this is that the work factor is exponential

when you increase the work factor by 1 the function becomes twice as slow here's a graph of decrypt hash time by work factor on my laptop the exponential increase is quite clear most folks recommend setting it to around 15 for real use cases which takes 1.3 seconds on my laptop fun fact when it was first published the

recommended work factor was just six which would take just two milliseconds on my modern laptop so is that it are we done is there an even higher tier s tier it's kind of a trick answer but there is s tier is not storing passwords at all as we've learned in this video storing passwords is quite tricky

so consider ways to avoid doing it at all for example you can use other authentication services like sign in with google or sign in with facebook and others so that users can log into your product using an established authentication platform not only is it more convenient for users

you get to sleep better at night knowing that your system doesn't have any passwords at all in it that's all i have for today let's recap first we looked at storing passwords in plain text which means anyone can easily access them so we considered encrypting them which is not ideal because their original form

can still be recovered we introduced hashing to make that impossible but we saw that people can pre-compute huge rainbow tables to quickly break passwords to counteract that we introduce salting which individualizes each password with a random string called the salt so that precomputed databases don't work

anymore unfortunately hardware is so fast that even without precomputed databases attackers can still try billions of guesses per second so we need to switch to deliberately slow password hashing functions that greatly decrease the rate of guesses finally we bypass the whole problem by
considering how to not store passwords at all i hope this was helpful if you enjoyed this video please consider sharing it with somebody else who might also enjoy it thanks again

chunks.text: the principle of least privilege also known as Access Control principle or the principle of least Authority is a cyber security approach and one of the Core Concepts of zero trust security that has become increasingly popular over the last few years for many companies it is now simply the default setting for

Effective modern security implementing the principle of least privilege ensures that individuals receive limited access rights to networks systems and applications by restricting user privileges to the minimum required for their tasks the risk of accidents errors or unauthorized activities is greatly

reduced consider this should your marketing managers have access to the software development environment absolutely not similarly should your software developers Access Financial information no by following the principle of leas privilege each user group is given only the permissions needed for their essential job

functions by preventing users from installing unauthorized applications the principle of least privilege limits the ability of malware to spread in addition it restricts lateral Network movement confining malware to the entry point and preventing it from launching attacks against other connect Ed devices by

protecting super user and administrator privileges the principle of list privilege diminishes the entry points a malicious actors can use to access sensitive data or carry out sophisticated attacks restricting access to sensitive information reduces the likelihood of unauthorized data exposure

or leaks if an account is compromised the damage is limited to the minimum permissions assigned to that account preventing widespread access limiting privileges help prevent accidental changes or deletions of critical system files and data by users who do not need such access with fewer permissions

granted it is easier to track an audit user activities enhancing accountability and oversight the principle of least privilege helps meet regulatory requirements and internal policies by restricting privileged account access providing a full audit TR of activities for compliance verification by granting

only needed access system performance and management can be optimized avoiding unnecessary complexity if you want to implement the least privilege in your it environment here are some best practices to get you on the right track conduct a comprehensive audit to identify all privileged accounts including passwords

SSH Keys password hashes and access keys this audit should cover on premises systems Cloud environments devops setups and endpoints eliminate any local admin privileges that are not essential ensure both human and nonhuman users only have the minimum privileges necessary to perform their tasks distinguish between

administrator accounts and standard user accounts isolate privileged user sessions to enhance security store the credentials of privileged administrator accounts in a digital Vault this step is crucial for securing and managing these accounts Implement a policy to rotate all administrator passwords immediately

after each use this practice helps invalidate any credentials that might have been captured by malicious software and mitigates the risk of attacks like pass the hash constantly monitor activities related to administrator accounts set up systems to detect and alert on any suspicious Behavior which

could indicate an ongoing Cyber attack Implement just in time access elevation allowing users to access privileged accounts or run privileged commands only temporarily and on an us needed basis regularly review all Cloud identity and access management permissions and entitlements across us as and gcp

environments remove any excessive permissions to ensure Cloud workloads have only the necessary access thanks for watching if you enjoyed this video and found it useful I invite you to like it share it with your connections and subscribe to Heim Doll's YouTube channel for more

title: Cookies vs Sessions vs JWT Authentication Explained | Web Security Simplified

chunks.text: You ever wonder how your favorite shopping site just knows what's in your cart? Or how you can close a social media tab, come back an hour later, and you're still logged in? Well, that's not magic. It's web authentication. And today, we're going to pull back the curtain on how the web remembers who you

are. We're going to break down the two heavyweights in this space, the classic session and the modern JWT. So, here's our game plan. We'll kick things off with the big question that every single web developer has to answer. Then we'll look at the classic solution, good old cookies and sessions. After that, we'll

jump into the modern world with JSON web tokens. We'll put them headtohead, cover the security rules you just can't skip, and wrap it all up by helping you figure out which one makes the most sense for your project. All right, let's dive right in. At the heart of all this is one fundamental challenge every single

person building for the web has to solve. Memory. I mean, think about it. The web by its very nature is completely forgetful. We call it stateless. Every time you click a link or refresh a page, it's like you're a total stranger. If we didn't have a way to fix this, you'd be logging in over and over and over again.

Can you imagine how annoying that would be? So, how do we solve this puzzle? It all boils down to this one word, authentication. You can think of it as the web's bouncer. It's the process that stands at the door and asks that one critical question. Who are you? Making sure only the right people get access to

the right places. So let's talk about the first big solution to this problem. The traditional way of doing things. We're talking about the tried andrue combo of cookies and sessions. This is what's known as a stateful solution, which is just a fancy way of saying the server has to do the remembering for

you. And honestly, the best way to get this is with a simple analogy. Think of it like a code check. You show up at a venue, you hand over your coat, that's your user data, and the server keeps it safe. In return, what do you get? A little ticket, right? A unique ID. You don't have to lug your code around all

night. You just need to hang on to that little ticket. So, how does this code check thing actually work in the digital world? Well, it's pretty straightforward. First, you log in, right? Then, the server creates a session for you. Think of it like a little locker on the server and stores

your info there. Then, it hands you back that little ticket, your session ID, tucked inside a cookie. From that moment on, every single time you talk to the server, your browser automatically flashes that ticket. The server just glances at the number, finds your locker, and boom, it knows exactly who

you are. Now, this approach has some really big pluses. The number one benefit, security. Your actual data, your coat, never leaves the server site. It's never exposed. The server also has complete control. It can tear up your ticket anytime it wants. So, if you log out or an admin decides to ban you, that

session is gone instantly. But there's always a butt, right? What happens when your app gets super popular and you need more than one server to handle all the traffic? Now, you've got a problem. Which server has your code? This is the big scalability problem. The fact that the server has to remember you that it's

stateful creates a ton of overhead and complexity, especially for huge modern apps. And that very problem, the scaling issue, leads us straight to our second contender. The modern approach known as JSON web tokens. You'll usually just hear them called JWTs. This method is the complete opposite. It's stateless

and it was designed from the ground up for the kind of massive distributed web we have today. To get your head around JWTs, let's use a new analogy. Forget the coat check. This time you've got a VIP backstage pass. And this really highlights the difference. The pass itself has all the important info

printed right on it. Your name, your access level when it expires. You carry it with you and any security guard, any server can just look at it, see that it's legit and wave you through. No need to check some master list. The process starts out pretty similar. You log in, but instead of the server creating a

file, it generates this signed token, your VIP pass, and puts your user data right inside it. Then it sends that token back to you. Now, it's your job to show that token with every request you make, usually in something called an authorization header. Any server that gets it can just check the digital

signature, confirm it's real, and you're in. The server doesn't have to remember a single thing. The advantages here are massive for modern applications because the server stores nothing. It's stateless which means you can scale almost infinitely. This is an absolute gamecher for microservices where you

might have dozens of little services that all need to know who you are. The tokens are also super portable and self-contained. Everything you need is right there in the token. But of course, there are trade-offs. What if someone steals your VIP pass? Well, until it expires, they can pretend to be you.

Revoking a JWT is really hard because there's no central place to just delete it. You have to wait for it to expire or build some complex workound. And another thing, if you try to stuff too much information into that token, it can get pretty big and that can actually slow down your whole application. Okay, so

we've seen both approaches, the good and the bad. Now, let's put them side by side in a proper showdown to make the differences crystal clear. You know, if you remember just one thing, let it be this. With sessions, the server is the one responsible for remembering everything. It keeps the state. With

JWTs, that whole responsibility gets pushed over to the client. The client holds the state inside the token. That's the core architectural decision you're making. This table really lays it all out. Sessions are stateful, which makes scaling them a real headache. But on the flip side, kicking someone out is

instant and easy. JWTs are stateless, so they scale beautifully. But revoking a token before it expires, oof, that's tricky and takes some extra engineering. See, it's that classic battle. Do you want more control or do you want easier scalability? Now, look, no matter which path you go down, some security rules

are just non-negotiable. These are the things you have to do, period. No matter what system you're building, first and foremost, always, always use HTTPS. That encrypts everything. If you're using cookies for sessions, you got to set the HTTP only and secure flags to protect them. With JWTs, don't ever put super

sensitive data in the payload and keep them small. A really crucial strategy for JWTs is using short-lived access tokens with longer lived refresh tokens. That way, if a token gets stolen, the damage is limited. And for any system, you have to have a solid logout plan and protect your login pages from getting

hammered by attackers. All right, we've gone through the theory, the pros and cons, the security essentials. So, now it's time for the final most important question. Which one is right for you? The general rule of thumb is pretty clear. You're probably going to lean towards sessions if you're

building a more traditional monolithic app. You know, where the front end and back end are all one big happy family. and they're definitely the winner if you need that power to instantly revoke someone's access, like an admin needing to ban a user right now. On the other hand, JWTs are almost certainly your

best bet if you're living in the modern world of microservices and distributed systems. They are the perfect fit for single page applications, for mobile apps, and really any situation where different services or APIs need to talk to each other without sharing some central database of sessions. And that

really brings us to the core takeaway here, which is summed up perfectly by this quote from Raul Junko. There is no single best solution. There's no magic bullet. It is all about understanding the trade-offs and picking the right tool for the job you are actually doing. So now the choice is yours. As you start

planning out your next big project, what's it going to be? Are you going to go for the tight server side control that sessions give you or the massive flexible scalability that comes with JWTs? The right answer? Well, it all depends on what you're building. Choose wisely.

title: How to Choose the Best Chart for Your Data Visualization: Ask Yourself These 3 Key Questions

chapters.label: What type of data are you working with?
What do you want to communicate?
Who is the audience and what do they need?

chunks.text: we live in a world that runs on data it's how Amazon and Netflix know which movies and products to recommend how Starbucks manages a global supply chain and how Uber connects drivers with passengers in real time but the thing is data skills aren't just for tech companies or professional analysts

anymore everyone works with data to some degree and everyone can benefit from data literacy skills in this video we're covering an important topic that will help you take your data literacy to the next level when it comes time to decide how to visualize a data set or which specific chart to use it's important to ask

yourself three key questions number one what type of data are you working with is it geospatial time series categorical hierarchical or something more specialized number two what exactly do you want to communicate are you showing a comparison a composition a relationship or a distribution and

number three Who is the audience and what they need are you sharing this with an analyst a manager executive or the general public how you answer these questions will help you determine which type of chart or visual is most appropriate given the context so let's unpack each of these in a bit more

detail so question one what type of data are you working with there are many flavors of data out there including common ones like time series geospatial categorical and hierarchical but you might might also come across some more unique and specialized types of data as well like financial statements textual

data funnel stages survey responses and much much more and the key takeaway here is that the type of data you're working with often helps determine which type of visual will best represent it some common examples include using maps for geospatial analysis line charts to show time series and bar or column charts for

categorical comparisons other more specialized examples include things like waterfall charts to track Financial balances ler scales to summarize survey responses even word clouds to visualize information from text-based documents question two is all about understanding what you want to

communicate whether it's a comparison composition distribution or relationship comparison visuals as the name suggests are used to compare values over time or across categories common visuals here include variations of bar and column charts along with line or area charts for showing time series and some less

common examples might be something like a funnel chart if you specifically want to show sequential stages like for example the number of applicants who made it through each round of a hiring process composition visuals are used to break down the component parts of a hole this is where you'll typically use

stacked bar or column charts pies and donuts stacked area charts for showing composition changes over time and maybe things like tree Maps or sun sunbursts if you're dealing with hierarchical data specifically distribution visuals are useful when you want to show the frequency of values within a series like

the Olympic Athlete example we talked about earlier in this course by far the most common and effective visual for showing distributions is the histogram but there are others as well like box and whisker charts density plots violin charts or heat maps and last but not least relationship visuals help you show

correlation between multiple variables this is typically done using Scatter Plots or variations like bubble charts but you might also use tools like a heat map or correlation Matrix to show a relationship as well now you might be feeling a little bit lost or overwhelmed given just how many types of visuals

exist but let me give you some peace of mind 90% of the time basic variations of bar column and line charts will be the simplest and clearest way to visualize your data so keep it simple avoid using complex or custom visuals unless you absolutely need to and make sure to prioritize Simplicity and Clarity over

Aesthetics and design that takes us to our third question who is the audience and what they need one of the most common mistakes that we see people make is that they design based on what they want to build not what Their audience needs to see designing effective visuals requires a level of empathy and an

title: Tree shaking in JavaScript (Optimize the bundle size of your application) | Complete Example + Setup

chunks.text: in this video I'll talk about a very interesting and important concept called tree shaking in JavaScript this concept can really improve your application's performance now before explaining tree shaking you must know what bundlers are in JavaScript you must have heard of webpack or rollup as a JavaScript

developer well they're exactly what we call bundlers bundlers are tools used to combine multiple JavaScript files into a single file called a bundle this bundle can then be used in a web application or website to reduce the number of HTTP requests needed to load the JavaScript code they reduce the number of HTTP

requests because when a web page loads the browser makes a separate HTTP request for each Javascript file referenced in the HTML this can slow down the page load time and increase the load on the server by using a bundler the JavaScript code is combined into a single file which means the browser only

needs to make one HTTP request to fetch the entire code base this can significantly improve the page load time and reduce the load on the server now bundlers can optimize your application in many ways one of which is called tree shaking so what is tree shaking tree shaking is a technique used by modern

JavaScript bundlers such as webpack or rollup to eliminate dead code from the final bundle dead code refers to parts of your JavaScript code base that are never executed or used in your application the process of tree shaking involves analyzing your code base and identifying which parts are actually

used and which parts are not the unused parts are then removed from the final bundle resulting in a smaller bundle size and improved performance so how to enable tree shaking using webpack to improve our application's performance for that let's see an example with some simple JavaScript code and minimal

title: Core Web Vitals Explained: LCP, INP & CLS

chunks.text: If you want to improve the performance of a website, the first question is always the same. What exactly should we measure? Core Web Vitals answer that question with three metrics that focus on loading, reusability, and responsiveness. In this video, I will walk through each one and show you what is actually happening

inside the browser. Core Web Vitals focus on three aspects of user experience. The first one is Largest Contentful Paint or LCP, which measures how quickly the main content appears. The second one is Cumulative Layout Shift or CLS, which measures how stable the page layout is. And the third

one is Interaction to Next Paint or INP, which measures how responsive the page feels when user interactively visit. In this video, I will explain each of them with a short visual animation, and then we will look at the simple before and after code example to see how those issues usually happen in real applications.

Let's start with Largest Contentful Paint or LCP. LCP measures the time it takes for the largest visible element in the viewport to finish rendering. Usually, this element is something like a hero image, a large heading, or the main content block. So, instead of asking when did the page start loading,

LCP asks a more meaningful question. When does the main content actually appears for the user? For good user experience, Google recommend keeping LCP under 2.5 seconds. Let's visualize how the browser calculate this. As the page loads, different elements start appear inside the viewport. At first, maybe a

small element appears. So, the browser treat that as a current Largest Contentful Paint candidate. Then a larger element appears, so the browser update the candidate. Finally, the largest element appears on the screen, and once that element finish rendering, the browser records the LCP time. So,

the LCP metric is basically the moment when the largest visible element finish painting in the viewport. Now, let's look at a common issue that slows this down. So, in this example, the page include a slow JavaScript file inside the header. It's called source.bundle.js. Because this script is

blocking, the browser has to stop parsing the HTML while the script downloads and executes. So, if you look at this bundle.js, it has a full block here that will slow down the JavaScript execution. The reason for this behavior is actually quite simple. JavaScript is allowed to modify the DOM. A script

could insert element, remove nodes, and change the structure of the page entirely. So, the browser cannot safely continue building the page until the script has finished running. As a result, the browser pause HTML parsing, downloading the script, execute it, and only then continue building the rest of

the page. And that creates a problem for our LCP element. Because the browser is blocked at the header, it cannot reach to the part of the HTML where the hero image appears, which means the image request only starts after the script finishes. So, the most important content on the page start loading later, and the

LCP time becomes much worse. So, as you can see in the LCP before HTML, the script is in the header and it's blocking the rest of the page from rendering. And we have a Largest Contentful element here, which is the image. And if we go to the browser and open up the LCP before example, you can

see the script is loading a bit, and then the hero image shows up, and you can see Largest Contentful Paint LCP has like 5.4 seconds. You can see that in the Chrome DevTools in the Performance tab. And by default, it has three core metric, and you can see the Largest Contentful Paint is really bad at this

stage. Now, let's compare that with the improved version. Instead of blocking the page, we mark the script with a defer attribute. This tells the browser that the script does not need to run immediately. It won't change the DOM element. The browser can continue parsing the HTML, build the DOM, and

download the script in parallel. The script will only execute after the HTML parsing is finished, which allows the page structure and important resource to load much earlier. We also preload the hero image, so the browser starts requesting it as early as possible. And also, we give the hero image a high

fetch priority, which tells the browser that this resource is especially important for the page. If you are curious about how preload works in more details, I actually made another video explaining preload, prefetch, and lazy loading. So, you can check them out after this one. And now, let's go back

to the browser and go back to demos. I'm cleaning up the metrics here and then doing the after load. So, you see the image immediately because it's preloaded. And then the page is still loading, and then you can see that there's a much better result on the LCP, Largest Contentful Paint, even the

JavaScript itself is as slow as before. With this small change, the main content appears much earlier, and the LCP score improves significantly. So, key idea for LCP is simple. Try not to block the browser from loading the most important content. Prioritize the main visual element and then delay everything that

is not critical. Now, let's talk about Cumulative Layout Shift or CLS. CLS measures how much visible content moves unexpectedly while the page is loading. You might have seen this before. You start reading something on the page, and suddenly the text jumps because an image load above it or an

advertisement has started appears. That movement creates a layout shift. The CLS adds up all these shift into a score. A good CLS score should stay under .1. Let's visualize how that works. Imagine a simple grid layout with several elements. At first, everything looks stable, but then one element suddenly

grows because an image loads and its size was not known earlier. When that happens, the surrounding elements have to move to make space for that element. That movement creates a layout shift. Then another element changed shape, maybe from a square to rectangle, and once again, the surrounding elements

have to move. Each of those movements contribute to a CLS score. Now, let's look at a typical example in code. chunks.text: A rag system produces answers by combining two steps, retrieval and generation. The quality of the final response depends on how relevant the retrieved information is and how accurately the model uses that information. Hello everyone, welcome back to logical lenses. In this video, we are going to look at how rag

evaluation works in a clear and structured way. We'll go through the key metrics that measure retrieval quality, grounding quality, and the final answer. So, let's get started. Let's start with traditional evaluation matrix. Blue or bilingual evaluation under study measures how many engrams in the

generated text also appears in the reference text. A 1 g is a single word. A 2 g is a pair of words and so on. Blue checks these overlaps and produces a score between zero and one. A higher score means the generated sentence closely follows the reference. For example, take the reference, the sky is

blue today. And the output, the sky looks blue today. In the output, four out of the five 1 gs, the sky, blue, and today match the reference. So the 1 g precision becomes 4th or 0.8 for the two gs. Two out of the four pairs, the sky and blue today also match the reference. So the 2 g precision

becomes almost half. Blue then takes the geometric mean of these precision and gives a combined score of about 0.63. Both sentences have the same length. So the brevity penalty equals. Now brevity penalty is always between 0 and one. and it simply reduces the blue score when the generated sentence is shorter than

the reference. So the final blue score for this example stays around 0.63. This is why blue became the standard for machine translation where these short word patterns are a strong signal of equality. All right. Next let's discuss rouge or recall oriented understudy for gisting evaluation. It measures how much

of the reference content appears in the generated output. Instead of focusing on matching phrases exactly, Rouge focuses on recall. That is how much of the important information is captured. This makes rouge especially useful for summarization where the phrasing can change but the core ideas must stay

intact. For example, consider the reference summary. The company achieved record profits and the generated summary. Record profits were reported this quarter. To calculate rouge one, we look at 1 g overlap. The keywords record and profits appear in both. So the generated summary captures two out of

the three important content words in the reference. That gives us a rouge one recall of 2x3 which is around 0.66. For rouge two, we look at two gram overlap. The reference has the pair record profits. The generated summary also contains the same pair. So, rouge two recall becomes one out of one, which

is one. Since the generated summary captures the main idea even with different phrasing, rouge assigns a strong score. This is why rouge became the go-to metric for summarization where meaning matters more than matching sentences word for word. All right. Now, let's look at F1 score.

It measures how many important elements in the generated answer match the reference. It works using precision and recall and then combines them into a single number. Precision tells us how many of the predicted items are correct. Recalls tells us how many of the correct items were captured. F1 is the harmonic

mean of these two giving a balanced score. This makes F1 useful for tasks where the correctness of specific pieces of information matters more than full sentence structure like question answering, extraction and classification. For example, take the question who discovered penicellin. Reference answer

is Alexander Fleming and the generated answer is Flleaming discovered it in 1928. Here the key element we care about is the entity Fleming which refers to the same person as Alexander Fleming. The model predicted one entity Fleming and it is correct. So the precision is one and the reference expected one

entity Alexander Fleming which is also present in the output. So the recall is also one. Combining these F1 becomes one. Even though the sentence is phrased differently, the correct factual element is present. So the F1 score is perfect. This makes F1 a strong metric for evaluating tasks where capturing the

right fact or entity is more important than matching the entire sentences. Okay. So traditional matrix like blue, rouge and F1 work well when there is a fixed reference answer and the goal is to match its wording or important elements. They are perfect for translation, summarization and extraction. But a rag

system works differently. It retrieves information first and then generates an answer from that information. So the quality of the final answer depends on both the retrieval step and the generation step. Because of this similarity based matrix are not enough. A rag system needs matrix that directly

evaluate how relevant the retrieved context is, how well the answer uses that context and how accurately the answer responds to the question. This brings us to the matrix that are used specifically for evaluating rag systems. So the first matrix here is context precision. Context precision measures

how much of the retrieved context is actually relevant to the question. If the system retrieves five chunks and only two out of them are useful, the precision is two out of five. A higher precision means the retriever brought in less noise. Example, if the query is who founded Tesla and the retriever brings

five chunks but only two talk about Elon Musk and Tesla's founding, then the context precision is 2 out of five which is 0.4. It tells us that the retriever pulled some relevant information but also a lot of unrelated content. Next, let's discuss context recall. It measures how much of the relevant

information the retriever managed to find. If there are three important chunks in the database and the retriever finds two of them, the recall is two out of three. Example, for the same query, if there are three chunks that contain the founding details of Tesla and the retriever returns two out of them, the

recall is 2x3 which is 0.66. It shows the retriever captured most of the required information but missed one useful chunk. All right. Now let's discuss answer relevance. Answer relevance measures how directly the generated answer responds to the user's question. This is usually done using embeddings to check how

closely the answer aligns with the query's meaning. For example, the question, what is a transformer model? We get a answer. A transformer is a neural network architecture based on attention. Both are semantically close. So, relevance will be high. Next one is faithfulness. Faithfulness checks

whether the answer is fully supported by the retrieved context. If a statement in the answer does not appear in the retrieved text, faithfulness goes down. For example, if the retrieved context mentions Tesla's founders and the answer adds a claim that isn't present in those chunks, faithfulness drops because the

answer is no longer grounded in the provided evidence. And the last one which we are going to discuss here is groundedness. Groundedness measures how well the answer uses the retrieved context instead of relying on the model's internal memory. If the answer copies or closely paraphrases relevant parts of

retrieved documents, groundedness is high. For example, if the retrieved chunk says Fleming discovered penicelline in 1928 and the answer says penicelline was discovered by Fleming in 1928. The grounding score is high because the answer is clearly based on the given evidence. These rag evaluation matrix like context

precision, context recall, answer relevance, faithfulness and groundedness give a good understanding of how well the system retrieved information and how accurately it used that information. But in practice, calculating these scores consistently is not always simple. Some of them can be computed with embeddings,

but others need deeper reasoning. For example, to check faithfulness, an evaluator has to read the question. the retrieved context and the answer together and decide whether the answer is fully supported. This is where LLM as a judge becomes useful. A large language model can act like an evaluator. It

reads everything, the query, the retrieved chunks and the final answer and then gives a score for grounding or relevance. Very similar to how a human would judge equality. To make all of this easier and standardize, the community built Ragas, a dedicated open-source framework for evaluating rag systems.

Ragas provide a structured way to compute rag evaluation matrix without manually building evaluators for each one. It uses embeddings for semantic comparisons and it uses LLM as a judge for evaluations that require deeper understanding. This helps capture meaning, grounding and factual alignment even when the

wording varies. Raas provides four main scores. Faithfulness which is whether the answer is fully supported by the retrieved context. Answer relevance which checks how well the answer addresses the question. context precision which checks how much of the retrieved context is actually relevant

and context recall which tells how much of the relevant information was successfully retrieved. These four matrix together give a clear and consistent picture of rag system quality. Rag system needs evaluation methods that look beyond surface level text similarity. Traditional matrix like

blue, rouge and f1 helps us understand wording, coverage and factual elements. But rag adds another layer through retrieval and grounding. Matrix such as context precision, context recall, answer relevance and faithfulness help evaluate these two steps clearly and frameworks like Ragas bring these

evaluation together into a simple consistent workflow supported by techniques like embeddings and LLM as a judge. With these tools, it becomes straightforward to identify where a rag system is strong and where it needs improvement. So that's all on rag evaluation. Thanks for watching. This is
